fields.meta_title: Affiliate Landing Page Builder With Tracked Links | Emergent
fields.meta_description: An affiliate landing page wins the click before the sale. See four examples and build one with a clear disclosure and tagged buttons.
fields.h1: Build an Affiliate Landing Page, Then Count Every Click
fields.hero_description: Build an affiliate landing page with a disclosure up top, a tracked link on every button, and a click log you own.
fields.features_heading: The Parts Between Your Reader and the Merchant
fields.features_subheading: The network credits the sale. Everything before it happens on your page, down to the button that sends each reader on.
fields.feature_1:
A tracking ID on every button

Name each spot on the page and Emergent gives its button a sub ID, such as stove-top. Where a network reports by sub ID, as impact.com does, you see which spot drove conversions.
fields.feature_2:
Comparison tables built from your notes

Paste test notes for each product and Emergent turns them into a table with one row per item and your verdict next to the price. Sort by price and each tagged button moves too.
fields.feature_3:
One disclosure, placed the same way

The FTC's Endorsement Guides ask for a disclosure that is hard to miss. Write your sentence once, and Emergent sets it under the headline of every review it builds for you.
fields.feature_4:
Outbound clicks saved as rows

Each outbound click lands as a row in a database you own, with the button, the sub ID, and the time. Read the rows by week, or send them to a spreadsheet tool over its API.
fields.feature_5:
Prices changed by one message

Change a price once by message, such as "Stove price is now $89." Emergent edits the table row and the button label together, and the old price is gone from the whole page.
fields.feature_6:
Your page as code you keep

Export the page and its click table to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Or keep it hosted on Emergent under your own domain (custom domains use credits) and edit it by prompt.

fields.usecase_heading: Affiliate Landing Page Examples by Format
fields.tab_content_1:
Disclosed up top, tagged on every button

Switchback Trail Notes reviews a single backpacking stove per page. A plain disclosure sits under the headline, above the first Check price button. Each of the review's three buttons carries its own tracking ID, with stove-top on the one under the disclosure. Every click is saved with the ID it used.
fields.tab_content_2:
The $149 grinder drew half of last week's clicks

Kettlebrook Coffee Guide compares three burr grinders under $200 in one table, each row with its own tagged button. Last week the table sent 812 readers to the store. The $149 Corvo Mill drew 406 of them, the $189 Strada S drew 270, and the $119 Pico drew 136, all counted in the page's click table.
fields.tab_content_3:
Each code revealed by a tap and logged

Tap Show code on Pantry Pick Deals and the Harvest Crate code appears, while the meal-kit store opens in a new tab through the tracked link. The reveal is logged against that code. SPRING15 came off the list this week under a rule the editor set: any code with no reveals in 30 days leaves the page.
fields.tab_content_4:
Paid search applicants go to a person first

Before anyone applies, Tallyfold's program page states the terms: a quarter of every referred subscription for 12 months, credited for 60 days after the click. Each applicant names a main traffic source. Anyone planning paid search ads goes to Odalys Reyes for review; the rest are approved by email with a tracking link.

fields.howto_title: How to Build an Affiliate Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to an affiliate landing page that readers can trust and networks can credit, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick one offer and one reader
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Add what the merchant's page cannot
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Write the disclosure in plain words
fields.howto_step_1_des: Choose a single product or program and the reader it suits, such as solo hikers who want a light stove. A page that recommends one thing to one kind of reader is easier to write, and easier to measure, than a roundup of a whole catalog.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Note the commission, the credit window after a click, and which traffic sources the terms allow. Plan the page and any ads inside those limits. Keep a copy of the terms with the date you read them, in case they change later.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write from use: test notes, your own photos, a comparison with the alternatives. Google's spam policies name original reviews, testing, and product comparisons as the value good affiliate pages add, and treat copied merchant descriptions as thin affiliation.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Use a sentence nobody can misread: "I earn a commission on purchases made through these links." Leave out jargon and vague labels: the test in the FTC's guides is whether an ordinary reader understands it.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Readers who arrive from search want the answer first. Put a two-line verdict and the main button near the top, with the reason the product won. Testing notes and the full comparison go underneath for readers who want to check your reasoning.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Open each button in a private browser window and confirm the merchant page loads with your tracking ID in the address bar. Then look for the test click in the network dashboard. A broken parameter loses the credit for every sale that follows it.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Compare clicks with sales each week
fields.howto_step_7_des: If your network reports conversions by sub ID, set the click table against that report one sub ID at a time. A button with plenty of clicks and few sales points at the offer or the price. A button nobody clicks points at where it sits. Change one thing, then compare again.

scope.evidence: H1 "Build an Affiliate Landing Page, Then Count Every Click"; hero "Build an affiliate landing page with a disclosure up top, a tracked link on every button, and a click log you own." (under 130 chars, primary, verb first); how-to description one sentence: "Seven steps to an affiliate landing page that readers can trust and networks can credit, then build it with Emergent."

intent.evidence: Top 10 is network how-tos and example galleries; the page defines the term (FAQ 1, bridge page), shows four formats under "Affiliate Landing Page Examples by Format" (review, comparison table, coupon, merchant program), gives a seven-step how-to, and answers the one usable PAA verbatim ("What is the best free landing page builder for affiliate marketing?"). Meta promise "See four examples" is delivered by the four tabs.

specificity.evidence: Affiliate vocabulary throughout: sub ID, credit window, rel=sponsored, thin affiliation, Show code reveal, "a quarter of every referred subscription for 12 months, credited for 60 days after the click".

openers.evidence: Every paragraph opens on a full sentence: "Give Emergent your affiliate links...", "Paste test notes...", "Switchback Trail Notes reviews...", "Before anyone applies...".

craft.evidence: QC Q2/Q5/Q7 clean; two long sentences flagged P2 (feature_5 33 words, howto_step_4_des 35 words) are under the block line.

voice.evidence: Plain, product-led sentences with concrete detail ("Stove price is now $89.", "SPRING15 came off the list this week"); no AI-tell vocabulary. Minor term drift between "tracking ID" and "sub ID" kept as a note.

truth.evidence: Unsourced statement about how affiliate networks report, in three fields: feature_1 "the network report shows which spot sent the buyer"; faq item 8 "The network then reports sales by sub ID."; howto_step_7_des "Set the click table against the network's sales report, sub ID by sub ID." No spec.domain_sources entry covers network sub ID reporting. FTC, Google spam policy, rel=sponsored, ClickBank bridge page and impact.com program page claims all match their sources; Emergent claims map to approved ids.

distinct.evidence: Own angle (disclosure, per-button sub IDs, click log vs network report, merchant program page); QC D2 clean; no sibling primary in headings.

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic questions, answer-first, no brand or file-format asks; PAA item verbatim (hubctl verbatim: ok); hub link in item 2; sibling links thank-you-page and 404-page; moat lines in items 3, 6, 9.

images.evidence: uc-1 disclosure above Check price, "stove-top", "3 of 3 buttons"; uc-2 bars 406/270/136 sum to 812, 50%; uc-3 CRATE40 revealed, SPRING15 Removed under "No reveals in 30 days"; uc-4 three Approved, Brightmark Media to Odalys Reyes, 25% for 12 months, 60 days. Alt counts match the drawings (three approved applicants, three grinder values).

findings.quote: the network report shows which spot sent the buyer
findings.issue: States as fact that the affiliate network's report breaks sales down by the sub ID on each button. That is a statement about third-party systems with no spec.domain_sources entry (the five sources cover ClickBank's bridge page, impact.com's program page, FTC 255.0, rel=sponsored and Google's spam policy), and it is not true of every program (some only accept a small set of tracking IDs, not free-form sub IDs per button).
findings.fix: Add a primary source for sub ID reporting (a network's own docs, e.g. ClickBank TID or impact.com SubId) to domain_sources and plan.claims_to_source, and scope the sentence to networks that support it ("networks that accept sub IDs, such as ..."), or cut the network half of the sentence.

findings.quote: The network then reports sales by sub ID.
findings.issue: Same unsourced claim about affiliate network reporting, in FAQ item 8 ("How do you track clicks on affiliate marketing landing pages?").
findings.fix: Fix with the same source and the same scoping as feature_1; keep the wording consistent across both fields.

findings.quote: Set the click table against the network's sales report, sub ID by sub ID.
findings.issue: The step presupposes the same unsourced fact (a network sales report broken down by sub ID).
findings.fix: Once the claim is sourced and scoped, align this step to it ("if your network reports by sub ID, ..."); otherwise compare at the level the network does report.

findings.quote: confirm the merchant page loads with your tracking ID in the address bar
findings.issue: Advice resting on an unsourced assumption: many networks redirect through their own domain and the merchant URL carries the network's click ID, not the affiliate's sub ID.
findings.fix: Say "confirm the link resolves through your tracking link to the merchant page" or name a network whose parameter does persist, with a source.
